segments.text: Hey friends, that night in the village it wasn’t an ordinary rain.
It felt as if the sky had torn apart.
Lightning kept flashing continuously.
The wind was so strong that several trees had started falling, and the river
had completely lost its calm.
It wasn’t just water flowing in it anymore—it felt like nature’s anger
was rushing through it.
And the most shocking thing was that in that terrifying river, a man was
drowning, shouting, “Help!
Help!” 🌧️⚡🌊 Somehow, he kept shouting for help.
Some villagers were nearby, but they were doing
nothing except watching—perhaps they couldn’t do anything.
For a moment, his face would appear above the water.
People would see him, and then the water would pull him down again.
Some of them even recognized him and said, “Hey, that’s Aditya!” “Bring a rope!
Someone bring a rope!” 🌊 Everyone was just shouting, but no one was able to help.
And here, Aditya’s breaths were fading.
Now he felt that maybe he wouldn’t survive.
Many questions began to run through his mind “I have always helped everyone.
I have always wished well for others.
And today, when I need help the most, when my child needs me… I can’t even
help myself.” 🌧️🌊 And while he was thinking all this, the water rose over him.
Now the only thing visible was his cap floating on the water.
Aditya was one of the kindest people in his village, yet this
still happened to him.
But the question is—why did something so bad happen to him even after being such
a good person?
So friends,
if you too have hurt yourself many times in life just to keep others happy… 🌊
If you are the kind of person who always stands up to solve everyone else’s
problems, but when it’s your turn, hardly anyone comes to help you… If you are
someone who struggles to say **“no,”** who feels guilty about it, and who
finds it difficult to set boundaries, then today’s story is for you.
And this is not just any ordinary story.
✨ Through this story, you will learn how to say **“no”**—without feeling
guilty, without damaging relationships, and without appearing selfish.
In today’s story, I will share
**five powerful lessons** that will make it much easier for you to say **no**.
And that’s not
all—by the end of the video, there’s also a lovely gift waiting for you.
🎁 So make sure you watch the video till the end, so that you can learn to say
this **two-letter word** which is easy to spell but often very difficult to say.
So, let’s start. Now let’s come back to **Aditya’s story**.
Aditya had been a very good child since childhood.
Everyone in the village used to praise him.
His village was small.
🌿 There were mud roads, fields, and Aditya—the favorite of everyone around.
Since childhood, Aditya had been taught that good boys never say **“no”**
to others.
In school, good children don’t refuse when someone asks for help with homework.
At home,
saying **“no”** wasn’t even an option, otherwise he would get scolded or beaten.
And the people around him—villagers and relatives—also said the same thing.
If someone asked a child to do some work and he did it,
he was considered a **good child**.
But the children who refused were seen as **bad or mischievous kids**.
That’s how the villagers looked at things.
But one day, something specific happened
that made this belief settle deeply in Aditya’s mind.
The story was this: Aditya’s friend had bought a new **bat**.
🏏 They all wanted to play cricket together, and Aditya really wanted
to play too. But his dad said, “No cricket right now.
Study first.” So, controlling his feelings, he sat down to study.
He studied for half an hour, and just when it was time for him to go and play,
some guests arrived at Aditya’s house.
As soon as the relatives came home, his family stopped him from going out.
When he tried to go outside, Aditya got a
little irritated because he really wanted to go and play.
But the moment he showed his irritation, he was angrily silenced.
He was told, “Don’t you have any manners?
Guests have come to the house
and you want to go out to play?” He was scolded in front of everyone.
And at that moment, a belief quietly settled inside
him—a small belief: “If I do things my way, people will get upset with me.
But if I listen to others and do what they say, I will be seen as a good person.”
Since then, that belief had planted a strong seed in his mind.
**Fast forward.** Years passed like this.
Aditya studied well like a good child, and now instead of just
farming on his parents’ land, he had started a small business.
He had around eight to ten cows that produced a good amount of milk.
From that milk, he made ghee and sold it to people.
And because he was such a kind person, many people would come to him for ghee.
Sometimes they would take it on credit, sometimes they wouldn’t even pay him back.
And not just that—whenever there was
any problem in the village, everyone would call **Aditya** to help.
Aditya happily went and helped people solve their problems.
He helped everyone a lot.
But no one really took him seriously.
People often made fun of him.
They didn’t value him and simply expected
that **Aditya would take care of it anyway**.
Many times, he would leave his own family to help others.
Instead of spending time with his own children,
he would end up giving his time to other people’s children.
Aditya had become very close friends with someone.
His name was **Vikram**.
Vikram was also a businessman in the village and owned more land than Aditya.
He grew rice, wheat, and different kinds of grains, which he sold in the market.
Vikram always kept Aditya with him.
Whenever he had to go somewhere,
he would take Aditya along, and many times he kept asking him for favors.
Sometimes he would ask Aditya to bring something, sometimes
to help lift heavy sacks, and sometimes he would come to Aditya’s house and
casually take away containers of ghee.
Money was never even discussed.
And Aditya never asked him for it either.
He would just think, “It’s okay, this much is normal in friendship.” And
like this, everything kept going loosely and casually.
Many times, his wife
and family had advised him that he should focus more on himself.
But Aditya didn’t feel that was right.
He believed he should
be there for everyone, otherwise what kind of person would he be?
But then came a year when the heat became unbearable.
It was so intense that because of it, Aditya’s cows and
buffaloes started falling sick, and the milk production dropped drastically.
His crops also didn’t grow properly that year, and financially Aditya’s
situation became very tight.
The ration at home started running low.
At that point, his wife clearly told him that he should ask
**Vikram** for help because Vikram would surely have plenty of grain.
But Aditya had always felt very awkward asking anyone for help.
But one evening, he finally gathered the courage
and said softly, “Vikram, this year my situation hasn’t been very good.
If I could get some grain, it would really help.” Vikram laughed and
replied, “Of course, you’ll get it, my friend.
I’ll give you as much as you need.
I’ll even give it to you for less than the market price.
I’m not trying to make a profit from you.
The market rate is 1,500, but I’ll give it to you for 1,200.”
Now hearing this, **Aditya** went silent for a second, because
at that moment he didn’t even have that much money.
He knew that Vikram’s warehouses were full of grain, and
for Vikram, giving a few sacks of grain wouldn’t have been a big deal.
Deep inside, Aditya felt a little hurt.
Many times when Vikram needed milk or ghee, Aditya
had given it to him just like that, without asking for anything in return.
He had never even talked about money before.
But today, even in such a situation, Vikram asked him for money.
Thoughts like these started coming into Aditya’s mind.
Then another voice appeared
in his head—the voice of his childhood self: “No, such thoughts only come
to bad people.
He is a good businessman; of course he will talk about money.
Maybe I’m just overthinking.” When he returned home, his wife asked,
“What happened?” Aditya smiled and said, “Everything is fine.
Don’t worry, I’ll manage something.” Aditya had a bike.
He sold that bike and somehow arranged the money.
Like this, that difficult time also passed.
Then the rainy season arrived again.
🌧️ During that rainy season,
Aditya’s son played a lot outside and ate a lot of street food.
Because of this, one morning his son started feeling very unwell.
He developed a high fever and vomited several times.
His condition became so bad that everyone in the family got scared.
And just then, the heavy rain started pouring.
🌧️ A **stormy rain** had started.
Aditya thought he would go to the doctor once the rain stopped.
But on one side, his son’s condition
was getting worse and worse, and on the other side, the rain kept getting heavier.
Finally, he decided that he had to take his son to the doctor no matter what.
His village was very small and there was no doctor there.
So he thought he would go with **Vikram**, who had his own car, and take his
child to the doctor in Vikram’s vehicle.
🚗🌧️ But when **Aditya** reached
**Vikram’s** house and explained the situation, Vikram clearly refused.
He said, “Brother, the storm is too strong.
Driving in this kind of weather isn’t safe.
Our lives could be in danger, so I can’t go.” When Aditya asked him for the car
keys, Vikram replied, “Brother,
it’s not safe for you either.” “It could lead to an accident.
You shouldn’t go.
Let’s somehow manage for today, and we’ll see tomorrow.” Hearing these words
from Vikram, Aditya’s heart suddenly felt very heavy.
That day, he saw a **selfish side of Vikram**—fear in his eyes, but
only for himself and his car.
There was no guilt, no concern for Aditya or his child—just fear.
Aditya felt very angry.
He felt like saying
a lot to Vikram, but he didn’t say anything because he was a good person.
He just smiled and said,
“It’s okay, I’ll go on foot.” Vikram stopped him and gave him an old lantern.
He said, “Brother, take this with you.
It will be very dark on the way.” And with that, Aditya
stepped out into the storm, worried and tense, walking through the heavy rain.
🌧️🪔 As he kept walking, all these thoughts—his child’s illness
and Vikram’s behavior—kept circling in Aditya’s mind again and again.
His mind wasn’t working properly.
Since time was short, instead of taking the main paved road, he chose the muddy
path near the river so he could reach the main road faster.
From there, he planned to get a vehicle and go to the
city, so he could bring a doctor back to the village.
Meanwhile, as he was walking along the muddy path, lost in tension, his
attention drifted for a moment.
His foot slipped, and he fell straight into the water.
He had fallen into the big
river in such a way that there was no one around to save him.
Aditya felt that maybe he wouldn’t survive now.
He prayed,
“God, please just take care of my child.” 🌧️🌊 He felt that everything was over.
In the storm, his voice slowly faded away, and he drowned.
The only thing left floating was his cap.
But that was not the end.
The next morning, when Aditya
opened his eyes, he saw that he was lying in a large, comfortable house.
Some people were around him, and there was a man standing nearby.
His clothes had been changed.
Aditya looked around and asked, “Where am I?”
“Thank God, you’re still on this earth.
You narrowly escaped,” someone said.
Aditya turned his head and saw a man standing there.
The man told him that people had found him lying unconscious near the riverbank.
Smiling, he added, “People know me as **Doctor Book**, so they assume I’m a
doctor.
Your luck was really good that you survived.” “You are here at my farmhouse.
Some of my caretakers have knowledge about medicines, so fortunately you were
saved.” While talking, Aditya suddenly remembered and exclaimed, “My son!
My son is very sick.
I need to go to him.” Doctor Book raised his hand and said, “Calm down.
You’ve just been given medicine.
In this condition, you cannot go anywhere.” He insisted, “No, I have to go.
My child is not well.
My village is near Wada.”
Doctor Book calmly replied, “You have drifted very far with the river.
Wada is about 25–30 kilometers from here.
It’s okay, I’ll take you there.” Aditya quickly said, “No, no, I’ll go myself.
Just arrange a vehicle for me.” But the doctor understood that Aditya’s condition
was serious, so he thought it was better to take him along personally.
As they were traveling on the way, their conversation began.
One by one, Doctor Book started asking
him questions—how did you drown, what happened?
Slowly, because Aditya was still under the effect of the medicine,
he began to share everything, explaining each detail little by little.
After hearing Aditya’s entire story, **Doctor Book** felt very sorry for him.
It reminded him of a time when he had been somewhat the
same, and because of that he had suffered many losses in his own life.
So, with empathy, he said to Aditya, “Do you know what illness you have?”
Aditya replied, “No.” The doctor said, “You have **Nice Guy Syndrome**.
People who always try to be good sometimes become so good
that, even if we never harm others, others end up hurting us and simply walk away.”
“That’s why you should stay away from this syndrome,” the doctor said.
Aditya replied, “No, no, it’s nothing like that.” Then **Doctor Book**
asked, “Do you feel uncomfortable refusing people?” Aditya smiled and said, “Yes.”
“When you say **no** to someone,
do you feel guilty?” Aditya replied, “Yes, many times.” “And many times you
don’t even feel like doing something, yet you still end up doing it for others?”
He said, “Yes.” The doctor continued, “It feels like you have no boundaries.
Anyone can come to you anytime, ask you for anything, and get work done from you.”
Aditya replied, “Yes.”
Smiling, **Doctor Book** said, “This is a classic case of **Nice Guy Syndrome**.
And maybe because you don’t
know how to say **no**, the value of your **yes** has also become very low.”
“Whenever you help people or do their work, at first
they must have thanked you and appreciated you a lot.
But now they probably don’t even say **thank you** anymore.
They just assume
that *Aditya will do it anyway.*” Hearing this, Aditya’s fingers began to tremble.
Tears formed in his eyes, because deep down he knew it was true.
He had noticed many times that people didn’t value him the way they should.
Doctor Book also felt a little emotional.
He raised three fingers and said, “Listen to me carefully.” “First thing—next time
whenever someone asks you for a favor or any work, don’t say **yes** immediately.
Take a pause.
You can take as long a pause as you need.
Don’t answer in a hurry at that very moment.
Ask for as much time as you need to think about
it.” “Five minutes, one day, even two days—take whatever time you need.
Second thing—before saying **yes**, ask yourself a few questions.
Are you saying yes while
respecting your own boundaries, or are you just saying it out of guilt?
Are you agreeing at the cost of harming yourself?
Will your **yes** benefit only the other person while causing you a loss?
Will it break your personal boundaries?”
“If the answer to those questions is **yes**, then maybe it’s important
for you to say **no**. And the third thing—calmly refuse.
Saying **no** will not be your weakness; it will become your strength.
It won’t break your
relationships; in fact, it will strengthen them—at least the good ones.” Doctor
Book explained to Aditya that always saying **yes** is not the right thing.
Sometimes, you must also learn how to say **no**.
“Especially if something is breaking your boundaries, making you feel
guilty, or making you feel bad—then you must take care of yourself.
You are a good person.” After saying this, **Doctor Book** dropped him near
his village.
Aditya smiled, thanked him, and said goodbye.
Then he quickly ran toward his home, because all he wanted was to see his
child.
As soon as he reached his home, he saw that everyone in the house was crying.
It seemed like they all believed that Aditya had not survived.
But the moment he arrived, the entire atmosphere in the house changed.
His wife ran toward him, hugged him tightly, and asked, “Where had you gone?”
Aditya told everyone everything that had happened.
Then when he went
to see his child, he noticed that his condition had already become normal.
Some of Aditya’s relatives had brought a
doctor and shown the child to him, and now the child was out of danger.
After seeing all this, Aditya finally felt relieved.
But inside him, a different kind of silence had settled.
He saw that **Vikram** was also there.
As soon as Vikram saw him, he said, “Are you crazy?
I told you that you shouldn’t go on foot.
There was a storm, yet you still went.
See, this is what happens when you don’t listen to me.” For the first time, Aditya
didn’t defend himself and didn’t try to justify anything.
He simply nodded his head and walked away.
A couple of days passed like this.
During those one or two days, Aditya kept thinking about what **Doctor Book** had
told him. He realized that he truly had no boundaries.
So he took a day or two to start deciding what his boundaries
should be—when he should give his time to others and when he shouldn’t.
He spent those days thinking carefully about these things.
After that, on the third day, Vikram came back to his house and said, “Hey
brother, how are things?
Come on, let’s go to the market.” Immediately, a voice inside Aditya
said, “Yes, let’s go.” But he raised his first finger and took a pause.
He took a deep breath and remembered that today he had decided to take care of his
cows and buffaloes, to bring medicine for them and help improve their health.
After taking that pause and a deep breath, he realized that this request was
outside his boundaries.
He didn’t feel like helping Vikram this time.
So, for the first time, he said **no** He said, “No, I can’t
go.” Vikram wasn’t used to hearing **no**, so he was a bit surprised and irritated.
He said, “Are you crazy or what?” 😮 “Why can’t you come?
I’m not going alone,” Vikram said.
Aditya replied, “No, brother.
I have work today.
I can’t come.” Hearing this **no**, Vikram got quite angry.
It felt strange to him, but he still insisted, “Come on, let’s go.
You can do your work later.
Looks like you’ve become very busy now.” But Aditya again said **no**.
This time his refusal
was so firm that Vikram understood that Aditya was not the same person anymore.
He had changed.
Vikram left from there in his car.
But Aditya still felt heavy at heart.
For the first time, he had said **no** to Vikram—his own friend.
It made him feel like he was becoming a bad person.
But just then, he remembered what **Doctor Book**
had said: *Feeling guilty doesn’t mean that you are becoming a bad person.*
Feeling guilty simply means that you are stepping out of your comfort
zone and setting boundaries for yourself.
That is not bad—it’s actually a good thing.
And if the friendship is genuine, it will grow stronger, not break.
After this, other
villagers also came to him many times and asked for his help for no real reason.
Sometimes, when Aditya had the time, he would still help them.
But when he didn’t have the time—when he was genuinely spending time with
his child, with his wife, or doing some work—he would say **no** to people.
Some people had even started speaking badly about Aditya behind his back.
But now it didn’t bother him at all.
He just remembered what **Doctor Book** had
said: saying **no** doesn’t break relationships; it strengthens them.
At least the good relationships would remain, and the ones that broke were
probably never real relationships to begin with.
Now, when Vikram came to him, instead of just taking
ghee or asking for something directly, Aditya didn’t refuse outright.
But he would say, “Look, brother, ghee is getting very expensive.
You can take it now, but make sure to pay me tomorrow.” And so, little
by little, things started changing the right way.
Aditya started setting boundaries.
He stopped giving things on credit and began taking proper payment from people.
Even Vikram realized
that this was no longer the old Aditya—he had become a new person.
The strange thing was that where Vikram
used to make fun of him before, he now took it very lightly.
Now Vikram had started taking Aditya seriously, and at first,
Aditya thought that his friendship with Vikram might get ruined.
But instead, Vikram became an even better friend.
Now, instead of asking
for help all the time, Vikram would come himself when he needed something.
One day, laughing, Vikram asked, “Aditya, you’re doing okay, right?” Aditya smiled
and said, “Yes, I’m doing fine.” Now see, friends, this
story holds **five practical lessons** that you need to understand.
**The first lesson:**
if you never say **no** to people, the value of your **yes** will be lost.
Just like with Aditya—people didn’t value him.
He helped others a lot, but they didn’t appreciate his efforts.
So the first lesson is this: **if you never say no, your yes has no value.** The
second lesson: **Guilt is not morality.** Many people misunderstand
this—they think that feeling guilty means they’ve done something wrong.
But that’s not true.
Guilt is often a habitual reaction we’ve developed over the years, a way
our system tries to stay “safe.” Feeling guilty doesn’t mean you’re being selfish.
It could simply
mean that you are breaking an old programming or pattern in yourself.
The third lesson: **Pause before you say Yes!** The simplest technique, which has
personally helped me a
lot, is this: if someone makes a request, don’t immediately say **yes**.
Take some time, think it through, and then respond.
The fourth lesson: **Create boundaries.** You must have some boundaries.
If you don’t create them,
people will keep pushing you around and taking advantage of you.
The fifth lesson: **Real friendship, survival,
honesty.** Many times, we think that if we say
**no**, our relationships will get ruined.
But in reality, saying **no** actually makes relationships better and stronger,
because you are being authentic—not fake.
In real life, when you stay true to yourself, your mental health stays
healthy, and you are able to maintain more genuine relationships with others.
And all these things I’m telling you are not random ideas.
These concepts are explained in a very powerful book called **No More Mr.
Nice Guy** by **Robert Glover**.
In this book, the term **Nice Guy
Syndrome** is used, which Doctor Book also mentioned.
These are
people who constantly sacrifice themselves in order to gain approval from others.
Nice guys are afraid of conflicts.
They secretly expect that if they stay “good,” everyone will treat them well.
But many times, that doesn’t happen.
This book shares many
powerful lessons that are very important to learn—especially if you are a nice guy.
By breaking **Nice Guy Syndrome**, you
can become wealthy, earn respect, and confidently ask for what you want.
